sections.html:
Three city offices touch your real estate tax, and each answers a different kind of question.

Your questionOfficePhone
Wrong assessment on a real estate billCity Assessor804-733-2333
Tax amount and whether it is paidTreasurer, City Hall, 135 N. Union St.804-733-2322
Current or delinquent balance, DMV stopBilling and Collections, 144 N. Sycamore St.804-733-2346
Tax relief for the elderly and for ex-service membersCommissioner of the Revenue804-733-2317

Pay on the city website, walk in to the Fiscal Management Office at 144 N. Sycamore Street, use the drop box outside it, or mail a check to P.O. Box 1271, Petersburg, VA 23804. Expect a 3 percent convenience fee if you use a credit card. An electronic check costs nothing extra.

The annual bill arrives as four installments, due September 30, December 31, March 30 and June 30.

The Land Book drives the schedule. A parcel's value is fixed on January 1, begins to count on July 1, and covers billing through the following June 30. The city FAQ quotes $1.22 per $100 of assessed value, a rate City Council revisits annually, so confirm yours on the bill.

  • September 30: first quarterly installment.
  • December 31: second installment.
  • March 30: third installment.
  • June 30: final installment.

Ahead of closing, request a payoff from Billing and Collections that adds in late charges.

Values are reset every other year using January 1 as the date. When a reassessment year arrives, owners whose figure changed receive a Change of Assessment Notice on January 28. Roughly 15,000 parcels are in the assessor's care, and every one is looked at each cycle even if its value stays put.

Appraisers sort the city into assessment neighborhoods and value homes in bulk, drawing on the sales comparison, income and cost approaches and software called AssessPro. Recent sales come first. A sale that was not at arm's length can be excluded, which covers family transfers, foreclosures, bank sales, estate sales and distressed deals driven by court orders or divorces.

So a deep discount on a house from an estate may not pull values down around you. Substantially complete new construction and renovations are added to the roll and billed as a supplement for the portion of the year after they were finished.

Petersburg has three steps: an office review with the City Assessor, then the Board of Equalization, then the Circuit Court.

  • Office review: file by March 1 of the assessment year, or inside 30 days of the change notice date.
  • Board of Equalization: file by April 1, or inside 60 days of the notice date. Three owners with real estate backgrounds sit on it, named by the circuit court judge.
  • Circuit Court: the last stop for owners who disagree with the board or missed earlier deadlines. No city form exists, and an attorney typically handles the filing.

Speak with an appraiser first. The review lets you verify the recorded square footage and features of your house. An assessor's request for income and expense data that you ignore can keep that data out of evidence later. The board begins from the presumption in Va. Code 58.1-3379 that the assessor is right, so arrive with comparable sales and facts about your own property.

sections.h2: Tax programs and the vacant building rule
sections.html:
Owners can apply for a rehabilitation credit, a damage abatement or land use status, and a long-vacant building must be registered.

  • Rehabilitation credit: for five years, the added value from improvements is exempt. Apply before work begins. The fee is $125 for a residence and $250 for commercial property.
  • Damage abatement: for a building unusable for at least 30 days where the loss lowered its value by $500 or more. You have six months from the damage to apply.
  • Land use: first-time and yearly applications are due May 1, and the fee is $500.

Under Sec. 22-140 of the city code, a building that has been empty for 12 months or longer has to be registered with the building code official. The yearly fee is $100, and the owner must explain how the building will be kept up and supply a rodent abatement plan. A vacant house headed to market should be checked against this rule first.

Any unpaid tax is taken from the money you receive at closing, because Virginia ranks that lien first until it is satisfied.

The purchaser, or a foreclosure trustee, must route proceeds to taxes and levies including penalties and interest, as Va. Code 58.1-3340 provides. Your contract decides how the current year is divided. Va. Code 58.1-802 adds a grantor's tax of 50 cents per $500 of value, and sellers normally carry it.

Owners with back taxes, an empty house, unaffordable repairs or an inherited property often weigh a direct sale. Even then the closing agent needs the city's payoff figure, so phone Billing and Collections before signing anything.

The city lies on the Appomattox River roughly 21 miles south of Richmond and had 33,458 residents in 2020. No county sits over it, so the city itself values property, collects other taxes through the Commissioner of the Revenue and Treasurer, and enforces building rules through its code office. Older housing is common here, so buyers will ask about the age and condition of a house.

sections.h2: What to have ready when you call
sections.html: City staff can help faster when you give them the address, the account or parcel number from your bill, and the name on the deed. If you are calling for a parent or a relative's estate, ask each office what paperwork it wants before it will discuss the account. When you reach Billing and Collections about a payoff, say the date you expect to close, because the figure changes as penalties and interest are added. If a DMV stop is on file for the owner, mention it so it can be cleared in the same conversation. Write down the name of the person you spoke with and the date.

Work through these in order. Phone Billing and Collections and request a payoff with late charges. Ask the Treasurer which of the four installments you have paid. If the house has stood empty for a year, learn whether it needs registering and whether a fee is due. Ask the Assessor if a supplemental bill is on its way for recent renovations. Finally, hand the closing agent every figure in writing. If any two offices give you different balances, ask both to put their number in an email so the title company can reconcile them before closing. Keep a copy of each payment confirmation. A lender or buyer may ask for proof that the earlier installments were paid, and a printed confirmation answers that question in seconds.

faqs.q: How often does Petersburg reassess real estate?
faqs.a: Every second year, with January 1 as the value date. Owners with a changed value get a notice on January 28 of that year.

faqs.q: What are Petersburg's real estate tax due dates?
faqs.a: Quarterly, on September 30, December 31, March 30 and June 30.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to appeal a Petersburg assessment?
faqs.a: For an office review, March 1 or 30 days from the notice. For the Board of Equalization, April 1 or 60 days from the notice.

faqs.q: Do I have to register a vacant house in Petersburg?
faqs.a: Yes, once a building has stood empty for 12 months or more. The yearly registry fee is $100.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Petersburg house with unpaid taxes?
faqs.a: Yes, the title company pays it from your proceeds. Call Billing and Collections, 804-733-2346, for a payoff first.
